summary: Defines managed objects for subnetworks using IEEE 802.4 Token Bus technology, as an experimental part of the MIB. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary:
A MIB is a catalogue: it tells a network manager what numbers a device holds and what they mean. This RFC adds the entries needed to manage Token Bus interfaces, the bus technology that passed a single token around a ring.

The entries cover what the interface is doing now, how it should be set up, and what has happened to it.

subtitle: A catalogue of SNMP-readable objects for watching and controlling IEEE 802.4 Token Bus network interfaces.

tldr.problem: SNMP can read and write values on a managed device, but it only knows about the objects a device's MIB module defines. Token Bus interfaces had no such definition, so they could not be managed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines an experimental part of the MIB with three tables, one row per Token Bus interface, holding the interface's state, its initialization parameters and its statistics.
tldr.outcome: It is a Historic document, and it was updated by RFC 1239. The objects live in the experimental part of the MIB tree.

facts.label: One octet time
facts.value: The time taken to transmit eight bits

today: RFC 1230 is a Historic document and has been updated by RFC 1239. It defines an experimental part of the MIB for Token Bus interfaces, a technology that has since left common use.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers and the Framework Around It
sections.content:
The memo defines an experimental portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets. In particular, it defines managed objects used for managing subnetworks which use the IEEE 802.4 Token Bus technology described in 802.4 Token-Passing Bus Access Method and Physical Layer Specifications, IEEE Standard 802.4.

The Internet-standard Network Management Framework consists of three components. RFC 1155 defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management, and RFC 1212 defines a more concise description mechanism which is wholly consistent with the SMI. RFC 1156 defines MIB-I, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols, and RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, an evolution of MIB-I based on implementation experience and new operational requirements. RFC 1157 defines SNMP, the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the MIB. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of ASN.1 defined in the SMI, and each object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name specifying an object type, and the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. The syntax defines the abstract data structure, and the encoding says how that structure is represented, which implicitly determines how the object is represented when transmitted on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP only works on things someone has written down. This RFC is one of those written-down lists, for a particular kind of network interface.

sections.title: Three Tables, One Entry per Interface
sections.content:
The memo defines three tables. The 802.4 Operational Table contains state and operational parameter information which is specific to 802.4 interfaces. The 802.4 Initialization Table contains the parameter information used by an 802.4 interface as the values to be assigned to its operational parameters upon initialization. The 802.4 Statistics Table contains 802.4 interface statistics. A managed system will have one entry in each of these tables for each of its 802.4 interfaces, and it is mandatory that systems having 802.4 interfaces implement all three tables in addition to the generic interfaces table and its generic extensions.

All the objects are registered in a single subtree within the experimental namespace, with the identifier dot4, and they apply to every interface which conforms to the IEEE 802.4 Token Bus Access Method. At present this means interfaces for which the ifType variable in the Internet-standard MIB has the value iso88024-tokenBus(8). For these interfaces the ifSpecific variable has the object identifier value dot4.

Two new datatypes, MacAddress and OctetTime, are introduced as textual conventions. These have no effect on the syntax or the semantics of any managed object: objects defined using them are always encoded by the rules that define their primitive type, so no change to the SMI or SNMP is needed to accommodate them. They are adopted for the convenience of readers and writers in pursuit of a concise and unambiguous specification. MacAddress is an octet string of six octets, a six octet address in the canonical order defined by IEEE 802.1a; a 16-bit address is represented by setting the upper four octets to all zeros, so AAFF is written 00000000AAFF. OctetTime is an integer holding a time interval in units of octet time, one octet time being the time taken to transmit eight bits, following the 802.4 convention of specifying time intervals that depend on the bandwidth of the media.

A few objects are defined with optional status, to allow experimentation to determine whether they are useful. If consensus is reached and a subsequent revision is placed in the Internet-standard MIB, these optional objects will either be removed or become mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: Three lists per interface: what is happening now, what it should start with, and a tally of events. The two new datatypes are only a shorthand for readers; they change nothing on the wire.

sections.title: The Operational Table: State, Commands and Parameters
sections.content:
The operational table's entry starts with dot4IfIndex, which has the same value as the ifIndex object for the same interface in the generic MIB. dot4Options reports the optional parts of the 802.4 specification in use by the station: 1 for Priority and 2 for Request-With-Response, with the value being the sum of those in use, and zero meaning no options are in use.

dot4State reports the current state of the interface, with the values other(1) for a state that is unknown, for example because of an error condition, offline(2), outOfRing(3), enteringRing(4) and inRing(5). dot4Commands is read-write, and setting it causes the station to change the state of the interface: no-op(1) does nothing, enterRing(2), exitRing(3), reset(4) and initialize(5), where initialize loads the operational parameters from the initialization parameters and the value of dot4InitInRingDesired decides whether the station tries to enter the logical ring immediately. The 802.4 specification suggests that a station remain offline after a remote network management reset until a local network management initialize is performed. When read, this object always has the value no-op(1).

dot4MacAddrLen indicates the size of MAC addresses interpreted by the station, either sixteenBit(1) or forty-eightBit(2). dot4NextStation is the MAC address of the station's successor in the logical ring, and dot4PreviousStation is the source MAC address of the last token addressed to this station.

The remaining objects are timing parameters measured in octet time. dot4SlotTime is the maximum time any station need wait for an immediate MAC-level response from another station, and its value must be the same in all stations on the 802.4 network. There are also objects for the last token rotation time, the high priority token hold time, the target rotation times for the four service classes and for ring maintenance, the ring maintenance timer initial value, and the minimum post-silence preamble length. Two integer objects carry ranges: dot4MaxInterSolicitCount runs from 16 to 255, and dot4MaxRetries from 0 to 7.
sections.plainLanguage: The state object says where the station is in the ring, and the command object is how a manager tells it to join, leave or restart.

sections.title: The Statistics Table
sections.content:
The statistics table holds counters for each 802.4 interface. They record how the token has moved and how the frames have fared. dot4StatsTokenPasses counts the times the station passed the token, and dot4StatsTokenHeards the times it heard a token. dot4StatsNoSuccessors counts the occasions on which the station found no successor to pass the token to, which is the signal to look for a new next station, and dot4StatsTokenPassFails counts the times it failed in passing the token to the next station.

dot4StatsNonSilences counts the occurrences of non-silence followed by silence in which a start delimiter was not detected. dot4StatsFcsErrors counts the frames received with an incorrect frame check sequence and the E-bit reset, and dot4StatsEbitErrors the frames received with the E-bit set in the end delimiter. dot4StatsFrameFrags counts the occurrences of receiving a start delimiter followed by another start delimiter, an invalid symbol sequence or silence, without an intervening end delimiter. dot4StatsFrameTooLongs counts the frames received that were larger than the media's maximum transmission unit. dot4StatsOverRuns counts the times a first-in first-out overrun was detected in the station, and dot4StatsDupAddresses the times the station detected another station using the same MAC address.

The memo also defines object identifiers for 802.4 interface tests, for use with the interface extensions test table, and for Token Bus interface chip sets. Among the test error codes is the value for a test that fails because the modem could not be initialized.
sections.plainLanguage: These counters are what a manager reads when a token bus is misbehaving: tokens lost, frames damaged, and two stations claiming the same address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says in one line that security issues are not discussed in it. It is a catalogue of managed objects for one LAN technology, and it offers no analysis of who may read or write them.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security at all.

items.title: 802.4 Operational Table
items.text: State and operational parameter information specific to 802.4 interfaces, one entry per interface.

items.title: 802.4 Initialization Table
items.text: The parameter values an 802.4 interface uses as the values assigned to its operational parameters when it starts up.

items.title: 802.4 Statistics Table
items.text: Counters of 802.4 interface statistics, one entry per interface.

viz.caption: Some of the counters a manager can read

items.title: Token passes and token heards
items.text: How many times the station passed the token, and how many times it heard one.

items.title: No successors
items.text: How often the station found nobody to pass the token to, which is the signal to look for a new next station.

items.title: Token pass failures
items.text: How many times the station failed in passing the token to the next station.

items.title: Frame check sequence errors
items.text: Frames received with an incorrect frame check sequence and the E-bit reset.

items.title: Frames too long
items.text: Frames received that were larger than the media's maximum transmission unit.

items.title: Duplicate addresses
items.text: How many times the station detected another station using the same MAC address.
